title: Empirical Evaluation of a Generate–Validate–Repair Loop for Intent→Network Configuration Using a Deterministic Reachability Validator
abstract: We study whether a generator–validator–repair (GVR) loop around a single LLM (gpt-5-mini) improves the rate of correct, safely executable network configurations synthesized from natural-language intents, compared to plain LLM generation. Following a preregistered paired design (cns-m2026-01) we evaluated 300 intent→configuration tasks (600 episodes total) generated deterministically and scored with an automated deterministic reachability validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). Baseline (plain-LLM) produced execution-validated correct configurations in 299/300 tasks (99.67%); the GVR (guarded) condition succeeded in 300/300 (100%). The paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.00333 (95% bootstrap percentile CI [0.00, 0.01]); exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.0. The preregistered primary hypothesis (10% absolute improvement) is not supported: baseline performance was near ceiling and the observed improvement is negligible and not statistically significant. We report confirmatory artifacts (execution manifest, scoring traces, contingency table) and discuss operational interpretation, ceiling effects, and external-validity limits. All experimental artifacts, hashes, and the mandatory Disclosure Statement are provided.

sections.introduction: Generative LLMs promise to simplify intent-driven NetOps by translating natural language goals into device configuration. Prior work has explored LLMs for network configuration generation and intent translation (e.g., NetConfEval) and architectures that insert verification gates or closed-loop checks around model proposals. However, rigorous empirical evidence quantifying how a generate–validate–repair (GVR) loop affects operational correctness under execution-level reachability constraints is limited. We preregistered a focused paired study (cns-m2026-01) to measure whether adding a deterministic reachability validator and a single automated repair step increases the proportion of intents that yield execution-validated, safely executable configurations versus plain LLM generation. Our contributions are: (1) a preregistered paired experiment executed end-to-end with deterministic task generation, LLM calls (gpt-5-mini), containerized execution/scoring, and auditable artifacts; (2) confirmatory analysis of N=300 paired tasks; (3) reproducible evidence showing a near-ceiling baseline and discussion of implications for when verification loops matter.
sections.related_work: We position this study relative to recent practical and architectural work on LLM-driven configuration and verifier-augmented systems. Representative closely related studies include NetConfEval (Wang et al., 2024), which benchmarks LLMs for configuration tasks; Raptis et al. (2026), which proposes validation pipelines for LLM-enabled intent management; and contract-enforced closed-loop architectures such as the Wheel of Intelligence that formalize proposer/verifier separation. We do not attempt comprehensive surveying here; these works motivated our focus on deterministic reachability validation as an operationally meaningful gate.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and experimental plan: The study is preregistered as cns-m2026-01. Design: paired binary outcome per intent (baseline vs guarded) with unit = intent and N=300. Primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline. Planned analyses, inclusion/exclusion rules, contamination filters, power/sensitivity plans, retry policy, and multiplicity control were frozen before execution (see preregistration SHA256 recorded in execution manifest). Data and task generation: 300 tasks were produced by a deterministic synthetic NetOps task generator and contamination filters were applied; task metadata and seeds are archived. Model and orchestration: all LLM calls used gpt-5-mini (provider recorded). The guarded condition implements a deterministic reachability validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) that checks for intent constraints and unintended reachability changes; when the validator failed the workflow allowed a single automated repair attempt per preregistration. Execution: the experiment executed 600 episodes (300 pairs) with model_calls_used = 301; provider traces, model responses, validator traces, and final execution-state snapshots were logged and hashed. Scoring: each episode yielded a binary execution-validated success flag (1 = configuration satisfies intent and shows no unintended reachability change, 0 = otherwise). The analysis executor paired_binary_analysis_v1 computed the preregistered estimand via an exact McNemar two-sided test and bootstrap CI.
sections.results: Primary confirmatory outcome: complete_pair_count = 300. Baseline successes = 299/300 (99.67%); guarded successes = 300/300 (100.0%). Paired contingency counts: n11 = 299, n10 = 1 (guarded=1, baseline=0), n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Estimated paired difference = 0.00333. Exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.0. Paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.00, 0.01] (bootstrap resamples = 10,000, seed = 1729). Missingness and technical failures: none (failed_episode_count = 0). Provider-call accounting: model_calls_used = 301; stage counts show shared_initial_generation = 300 and repair = 1 (one repair call occurred as recorded in the execution manifest). Secondary and exploratory summaries pre-specified in the analysis plan (repair-iteration histogram, failure-mode contingency) are provided in archived artifacts; no substantive discordant patterns beyond the single guarded-only success were observed.
sections.discussion: Interpretation: the observed baseline performance was already near-perfect on the selected task corpus, producing a pronounced ceiling effect that leaves little room for measurable improvement from the evaluated single-step GVR intervention. The one discordant case (guarded success where baseline failed) shows that the GVR pipeline can correct isolated generator mistakes, but such cases were rare in this dataset. Consequently, the preregistered primary hypothesis (targeting a 10% absolute improvement) is not supported. Operational implication: verification/repair gates are most likely to materially improve correctness when baseline generator error rates are appreciable (well above the near-zero error observed here), or when task distributions include harder or more ambiguous intents. Threats to validity: internal—deterministic task generation and single-model evaluation limit generality; construct—the validator operationalizes safety as absence of unintended reachability changes in the emulated environment (a defensible but partial construct of operational safety); external—results do not necessarily generalize to in-the-wild human-written intents, different LLMs, or production devices. We do not claim superiority of any architectural pattern beyond the observed empirical outcome on this task corpus.
sections.conclusion: A single-LLM GVR loop with a deterministic reachability validator produced one additional success out of 300 paired tasks relative to plain-LLM generation; the small absolute change and statistical test (p = 1.0) indicate no confirmatory evidence that the evaluated GVR intervention meaningfully increases correct, execution-validated configurations on this task corpus. The experiment is fully archived with raw responses, validator traces, and hashes. Future work should (a) evaluate on more challenging, contaminated, or human-authored intents that produce higher baseline error rates; (b) compare multi-iteration repair loops and stronger validators; and (c) measure cost–benefit tradeoffs in operationally realistic deployments.

limitations: Ceiling effect: baseline (plain-LLM) success was 299/300, limiting measurable improvement by the evaluated single-step GVR loop.
Task scope: tasks were deterministically generated synthetic intent→configuration items; results may not generalize to diverse human-authored intents or to entailed real-world operational complexity.
Model scope: single-model evaluation (gpt-5-mini) — conclusions do not necessarily transfer across model families or safety-calibrated variants.
Validator construct: safety defined as absence of unintended reachability changes in the emulated environment; this is a practical but partial operationalization of NetOps safety.
Repair budget: the experiment allowed at most one automated repair per task (per preregistration); multi-iteration repair behavior was not explored in this confirmatory run.
